title: Analyzing activity and injury: lessons learned from the acute:chronic workload ratio
authors: Wang C, Vargas JT, Stokes T, Steele R, Shrier I
population: Methodological review of ACWR analysis (no participants)
findings: The IOC has recommended ACWR with thresholds, but limitations of the ratio and of how it has been analysed affect the validity of those recommendations and should discourage its use.
Using exponentially weighted moving averages to calculate ACWR creates an initial load problem, and is inapplicable to sports where athletes taper their activity.
Implementation problems include discretisation, sparse data, bias in injured athletes, unmeasured and time-varying confounding, and application to subsequent injuries.
Proposes causal-inference based analytic strategies as alternatives, conditional on well-conceived study design.
limitations: Methodological critique, not an empirical study; no effect sizes; alternatives are conditional on good study design.
implications: Because the engine tapers before races, suppress any ratio-based warnings or display in taper and recovery weeks.
Any ACWR display needs a warm-up period (initial load problem); the 4-week minimum is an engineering default, not from the paper.
Avoid fixed ratio bands as hard rules.

verification.notes: Crossref: Sports Med 50:1243-1254 (online Mar 2020). Abstract matched. The '4 weeks' figure in the implication is flagged as an engineering default.
